meaning: A network built mainly from convolution layers, which slide small learned filters over an image. Locality and weight sharing make it tiny compared with an MLP and let it detect a pattern anywhere.
The prior that a pixel is best understood from its neighbours first: each conv output looks only at a small k × k patch of the layer below.
Using the same filter weights at every position of the image. It makes a conv layer's parameter count independent of the image size (64 filters of 3 × 3 × 3 = 1,792 parameters at any size).

Equivariant: shift the input and the feature map shifts the same way (convolution). Invariant: the output doesn't change at all when the input shifts (approximately achieved by pooling, especially global pooling).
The small grid of learned weights a convolution slides over its input, k × k × C_in numbers. Each position's output is the dot product of the kernel with the patch under it.
The output grid of one conv channel: how strongly its pattern appears at each position.
How many pixels the kernel jumps between positions. Stride 2 roughly halves the output size in each direction and cuts later compute by 4.
A border of (usually zero) values added around the input. “Valid” = no padding, the output shrinks by k − 1; “same” = p = (k − 1)/2, the output keeps the input size at stride 1.
Output side = ⌊(n + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1 for input side n, kernel k, padding p, stride s (with dilation d, replace k by d·(k − 1) + 1).
The depth of an image or feature map: 3 for RGB, then one per filter. A conv has one k × k × C_in kernel per output channel; parameters = k·k·C_in·C_out + C_out.
A conv that looks at one pixel's channel vector: a small dense layer applied at every position. Used to mix or squeeze channels cheaply (256 → 64 for 16,448 parameters).
Sliding a kernel without flipping it. Deep-learning “convolutions” are actually cross-correlations; with learned kernels the difference doesn't matter.
The input region that can affect a unit. Grows by (k − 1) × (product of earlier strides) per layer: stacking adds, striding and pooling multiply.
The part of the receptive field that actually has much influence: roughly Gaussian and much smaller than the theoretical one (Luo et al. 2016).
Replacing each window (often 2 × 2, stride 2) with its maximum or mean, per channel. No parameters; shrinks the map and adds small-shift tolerance.
Averaging each channel's whole feature map into one number, so 7 × 7 × 512 becomes 512. The standard zero-parameter CNN head, which works for any input size (Network in Network, 2013).

A convolution whose kernel taps are spaced d pixels apart, covering a wider area with the same weights and no loss of resolution. Stacking dilations 1, 2, 4, 8 grows the receptive field exponentially.
The feature-extracting body of a vision network (e.g. ResNet-50 without its head), reused for classification, detection, segmentation and transfer learning.
A CNN made of blocks that output x + F(x). The shortcut solved the degradation problem and allowed 152-layer networks (ILSVRC 2015 winner).
1 × 1 conv to fewer channels, 3 × 3 conv, 1 × 1 back up: the same output for far fewer parameters and multiply-adds than a 3 × 3 at full width. Used in GoogLeNet-style modules and deep ResNets.
A per-channel k × k (depthwise) conv followed by a 1 × 1 (pointwise) conv. Costs 1/N + 1/k² of a standard conv, about 8–9× less at 3 × 3 (MobileNet).
EfficientNet's rule: grow depth, width and input resolution together by fixed factors (1.2, 1.1, 1.15 per step) instead of one at a time.
Starting from a network pre-trained on a large dataset and adapting it to a new task, usually with a new head. Works because early features (edges, textures) are general.
Feature extraction freezes the backbone and trains only a new head; fine-tuning also updates some or all backbone layers, usually with a smaller learning rate.
Different learning rates per layer group: highest for the new head, lower for deeper (closer to the input) layers, so pre-trained features aren't wrecked (ULMFiT: ÷ 2.6 per layer).
How different your images are from the pre-training images (e.g. X-rays vs everyday photos). The bigger the gap, the less frozen features help and the more you need to fine-tune.
Hiding parts of the image with a patch and measuring the drop in the class score, to find the regions a decision depends on (Zeiler & Fergus 2013). The patch colour must mean “absent” for your data.

Saliency: the gradient of a class score with respect to each pixel. Grad-CAM: last conv layer maps weighted by their average gradient, through ReLU, giving a coarse class-specific heatmap. Sanity-check either one.
ImageNet-trained CNNs rely more on texture than shape: a cat shape with elephant skin is classified as an elephant (Geirhos et al. 2018). Humans do the opposite.
